name: Curvularia leaf spot
summary: A Florida hemp leaf-spot disease supported by isolation, morphology, three-locus sequence evidence, repeated pathogenicity testing, and reisolation. Yellow spots on young or old leaves can become tan to brown with yellow halos, but this shared leaf-spot phenotype cannot establish Curvularia pseudobrachyspora from images alone.
affectedParts: lower leaf surface for paired inspection
whole plant and neighboring plants for distribution context
stages: one-month-old field hemp in the Florida report
five-week-old greenhouse plants in pathogenicity testing
indicators: The reported field phenotype began as small yellow spots on both young and old hemp leaves.
Spots progressed to tan or brown lesions surrounded by yellow halos, a pattern shared with several other foliar diseases.

The institutional Figure 4 reference shows numerous discrete to locally merging lesions across one detached hemp leaf and supplies whole-leaf distribution context rather than a universal progression sequence.
Paired upper- and lower-surface views are needed because one institutional upper-surface-style view cannot exclude underside sporulation, arthropods, residue, or an oomycete differential.
Representative lesion-edge isolates in the primary report produced sparse aerial mycelium, fimbriate colony margins, and pale-gray or gray-olivaceous-to-brown zones.
Compatible conidia were mostly curved, ellipsoidal to obovoid, pale brown to brown, two- to three-distoseptate, and borne in groups from geniculate conidiophores; trained microscopy is required.
Three-locus ITS, GAPDH, and EF1-alpha evidence plus phylogenetic analysis supported C. pseudobrachyspora for three isolates, while a fourth isolate raised a cryptic-species warning.
Repeated inoculation reproduced comparable leaf spots after two weeks and reisolation linked the organism to symptoms while water-treated controls stayed healthy.
exclusions: Black pinhead pycnidia embedded in lesion centers with compatible plant-linked testing support Septoria rather than Curvularia.
Pale tan or white centers with conspicuous melanized conidiophore fascicles and compatible testing support Cercospora.
Gray-brown velvety or sooty lower-surface patches following veins support Pseudocercospora as a differential.
Dark gray or black fuzzy sporulation on both surfaces and a compatible Bipolaris isolate support Bipolaris leaf spot.
Concentric target-like rings or compatible Alternaria structures and sequence evidence support Alternaria.
Water-soaked or angular lesions, bacterial streaming or ooze, and plant-linked bacterial identification support bacterial leaf spot.
Purple-to-gray underside growth with corresponding angular upper-surface chlorosis and oomycete testing supports downy mildew.
Mites, thrips, eggs, frass, webbing, chewing evidence, or punctures without lesion-linked fungal evidence support arthropod injury.
A sharp spray, light, aisle, contact, or weather boundary with negative representative lesion testing supports abiotic injury.
Conidium size, a single locus match, or a grouped accession list is used to assign an exact species or isolate without specimen-linked multilocus interpretation.

progression.description: Record cultivar, plant age, canopy position, neighboring plants, both leaf surfaces, and matched apparently healthy leaves before interpreting spots.
Small yellow spots appear on young or old leaves; tag the same leaves because this stage is visually nonspecific.
Spots become tan to brown while retaining a yellow halo; capture scale, lesion count, distribution, and both surfaces.
Additional lesions or locally merging necrotic areas can involve more of the leaf; do not convert the trial-specific incidence or damage observations into a universal severity threshold.
A confirmed label requires lesion-linked isolation, compatible morphology and multilocus evidence, plus pathogenicity evidence when causality must be established.

lookAlikes: Xanthomonas or another bacterial leaf spot
Nutrient, salinity, drought, or root-zone stress
confirmation: Capture the whole plant, canopy neighborhood, full leaf, and matched upper- and lower-surface close-ups with a scale and stable plant and lesion identifiers.
Revisit tagged leaves to distinguish new yellow spots and lesion expansion from fixed spray marks, old injury, or unrelated holes.
Collect multiple fresh representative lesions, including active margins, before saprophytes dominate; retain cultivar, age, field position, recent weather, irrigation, and foliar-input metadata.
Use lesion-edge isolation and trained examination of colony, conidiophore, and conidium morphology while recording every organism recovered from the sample.

Keep field-lesion, culture-plate, and inoculated-plant captures in separate observation contexts linked by plant, lesion and isolate IDs; label plate images with medium, incubation temperature, light cycle and culture age. The reported 25 degrees C and 12-hour light/12-hour dark cycle describe initial isolation, not a field climate diagnostic rule.

Preserve the field variety names separately from greenhouse Puma-3 and record any nearby goosegrass as contextual scouting data, not a confirmed reservoir. Resolving a transmission-source claim requires linked plant/weed sampling and specialist evidence beyond proximity.

For species-level confirmation, link the photographed plant and lesion to validated multilocus evidence including ITS, GAPDH, and EF1-alpha or an equivalently resolving current method; ITS or appearance alone is insufficient.
Interpret divergent isolates cautiously because one isolate in the first report raised a cryptic-species possibility despite similarity to C. pseudobrachyspora.

Capture calibrated microscopy of lesion-linked cultures with scale bars, conidial length and width, septation, middle-cell pigmentation, conidiophore origin and measurement count. Keep the reported 25-conidium size range as study context, not an identification threshold.

Link plant, tagged lesion, culture and sequence IDs at each locus; retain chromatograms or laboratory reports and accession-to-isolate mapping. Do not manufacture individual mappings from the published grouped GenBank ranges, especially for divergent isolate 19-405.
When causality is required, retain symptom reproduction, reisolation, and negative controls linked to the isolate; organism detection alone does not prove that every visible lesion was caused by it.

Keep symptom-only, detached-leaf-only, mixed-pathogen, culture-unlinked, single-locus-only, low-resolution, generated, vendor, anecdotal, forum, and rights-unclear samples out of confirmed labels and route unresolved evidence to review.
immediateActions: Tag and photograph representative plants before removing tissue, preserving field and canopy distribution.
Limit movement of symptomatic propagation material and retain fresh, traceable lesions for a plant diagnostic laboratory.
Map affected plants against cultivar blocks, splash or irrigation zones, leaf wetness, airflow, recent foliar applications, and mechanical or weather injury.
correctivePlan: Base management on the organism confirmed from representative plant-linked lesions and on current crop, site, and jurisdiction requirements.
Track new lesion incidence on tagged plants after sanitation or environmental changes; persistent old lesions do not measure treatment success.
Reassess the diagnosis when new lesions do not match the documented sequence or repeated representative tests do not support Curvularia.
prevention: Use clean propagation material and avoid moving symptomatic leaves, residue, tools, or splash water into clean production areas.
Reduce avoidable prolonged leaf wetness and retain adequate spacing and airflow where production constraints allow.
Scout young and old leaves with stable plant IDs, paired surfaces, and repeated views so nonspecific yellow spots are not prematurely labeled.
warnings: Yellow spots, tan-to-brown centers, yellow halos, and leaf-level lesion abundance are not individually or jointly species-specific in an image.

The primary report covers one Florida field trial, four selected isolates, defined cultivars, and a small controlled inoculation; it does not establish universal prevalence, susceptibility, timing, yield loss, or thresholds.

Pumma-2 in the field account and Puma-3 in the inoculation assay are distinct reported labels, not interchangeable spellings; goosegrass is a proposed alternative host, not a demonstrated local transmission source. Unresolved cultivar or reservoir assignments require review.

The 72-hour bagging exposure and two-week symptom endpoint belong to an artificial inoculation assay, not an untreated field time series. Matching those times or conidial dimensions alone cannot confirm an image; incomplete isolate-to-sequence linkage requires human review.
One isolate was phylogenetically differentiated from the other three and may represent a cryptic species, so species labels require isolate-linked multilocus interpretation.

UF/IFAS Figure 4 is an attributed institutional whole-leaf differential, not a plant- and lesion-linked laboratory record; its CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 license prohibits derivatives and commercial reuse without permission.
The reference lacks a scale, paired underside, whole-plant distribution, sample identifier, culture, microscopy, sequence accessions, and pathogenicity linkage for the pictured leaf.
All unresolved symptom-only, detached, mixed-organism, unlinked-laboratory, single-locus-only, low-resolution, and rights-unclear samples retain review flags.

sources.title: First Report of Curvularia pseudobrachyspora Causing Leaf Spot on Hemp (Cannabis sativa) in Florida
supportedClaims: In one October-to-December 2019 Wimauma, Florida field trial, small yellow spots occurred on young and old leaves of one-month-old hemp and developed into tan-to-brown spots with yellow halos; field incidence, damage, varieties, and timing are study-specific observations.

Four single-spored isolates were characterized by colony and conidial morphology plus ITS, GAPDH, and EF1-alpha sequences; three grouped closely with Curvularia pseudobrachyspora while one diverged enough to raise a cryptic-species possibility.

Spray inoculation of four five-week-old Puma-3 plants per isolate reproduced leaf spots after two weeks, water controls remained healthy, and the organism was reisolated; the experiment was repeated once.

The report states that epidemiology and management require additional study, so the Florida observations do not establish universal cultivar susceptibility, field prevalence, progression timing, or action thresholds.

The report measured 25 conidia: length 20.3–31.7 micrometers and width 9.5–15.9 micrometers, with middle cells larger and darker than the others. These culture observations support trained microscopy, not a species cutoff or camera-visible leaf diagnosis.

Reported GenBank groups are ITS MT071994 and MT072019–MT072021, GAPDH MT085362–MT085365, and EF1-alpha MT085366–MT085369. Isolates 19-407, 19-409 and 19-410 grouped closely with C. pseudobrachyspora, while 19-405 was differentiated phylogenetically; the grouped accession list alone does not specify every isolate-to-locus pairing.

The pathogenicity assay used 100,000 spores/mL in 0.01% Tween 20 and bagged inoculated plants for 72 hours; sterile-water controls received the same conditions. The two-week symptom observation is an assay endpoint, not a field incubation or video-progression standard.

Initial isolation used surface-disinfested leaf tissue on general isolation medium at 25 degrees C with a 12-hour light/12-hour dark cycle. These are laboratory culture conditions, not demonstrated field infection requirements.

Field varieties included Pumma-2, Eletta Campana, Carmagnola Selezionata and Tygra; the inoculation test used Puma-3. Preserve those distinct reported names and settings rather than inferring a replicated cultivar-susceptibility ranking.

The authors cite prior reports on areca palm and goosegrass but propose goosegrass only as a possible alternative host. Dataset inference: nearby weeds or a shared host report do not establish the source of a photographed hemp infection.

sources.title: Field Guide to Hemp (Cannabis sativa) Diseases
sources.publisher: University of Florida Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences Extension
supportedClaims: The UF/IFAS field guide describes Curvularia spots on young and old hemp leaves as yellow spots that become tan to brown with a yellow halo and explicitly notes visual confusion with Cercospora and Septoria.

UF/IFAS Figure 4 is an institutional hemp-leaf reference credited to Marcus Marin, Jacqueline Coburn, Johan Desaeger, and Natalia Peres; its CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 license limits reuse to unchanged noncommercial display with attribution.

The guide recommends plant-diagnostic-center identification and confirmation, so Figure 4 supplies bounded whole-leaf differential context rather than laboratory ground truth for an individual dataset sample.
